title: Pretrees
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: Sets with a betweenness relation that behaves as in a tree. The first lesson gives the four axioms of a pretree, their consequences for four points, intervals, and the theorem that every finite pretree is a set of vertices of a finite tree with the betweenness of the tree, by an explicit construction from adjacent points and maximal cliques. It follows that linear sets have exactly two directions, that intervals are ordered, and that three points have at most one median. The second lesson treats dense, complete and median pretrees: a half-open interval of a dense pretree determines its open end; a complete dense pretree need not be median (an explicit example); in dense median pretrees an interval [x,y) inside [x,z] has y in [x,z]; and in complete dense median pretrees every cut of an interval is made at a point, so that intervals are ordered sets without gaps. The third lesson defines separable median pretrees, shows that a weakly dense set becomes strongly dense when medians are added, proves Cantor's theorem on countable dense orders, and concludes that in a complete separable median pretree every interval is ordered like the real interval [0,1]. The fourth lesson proves that a compact space with a countable dense subset and a complete dense median pretree structure whose sets H(x,y) are open is a dendrite, in which the intervals of the pretree are the only arcs. Pretrees are the structure carried by the cut points of a continuum; they are used in OpenAI's proof (2026) of the Singer conjecture in dimension four outside the middle degree.
prerequisites: graphs, paths, cycles and connected graphs (definitions only)
for the fourth lesson: the course Continua, arcs and cut points (arcs, dendrites) and the Urysohn metrization theorem (core course Point-Set Topology)
the course proves every other fact it uses

checks.reading: Written on 11 Oct 2026 against Section 2 of Bowditch's memoir (author's version, library copy free/authors/bowditch/bhb-treelike.pdf, pages 10-14 read as page images). The embedding of finite pretrees in finite trees is proved by a construction different from the memoir's induction: the tree is built from the adjacency graph, with one new vertex for every maximal clique of at least three points. Each proof was re-read step by step; three slips were corrected (a wrong lemma citation, a missing clause, an inconsistent exercise). Lesson 2 was written against pages 15-16 of the memoir. Its Lemmas 2.8, 2.10 and 2.11 are false as stated: the lesson gives a counterexample (a tripod with a half-open segment next to the centre removed is complete and dense but not median) and proves the first two with the hypothesis 'median' added; findings ledger F-0011. Lesson 3 was written against page 16 of the memoir (Lemmas 2.12 and 2.13); the proof of Lemma 2.12 is written out with gates in a finite tree, and Cantor's theorem is proved. Lesson 4 was written against pages 17-18 of the memoir (Theorem 2.14, Lemmas 2.15-2.19) with the hypothesis 'median' stated; the countable base is proved from the sets H(p,q) directly, and every statement about medians is checked by gates in a finite tree.
checks.layout: Measured in the staged pages at column widths 1100, 768, 543 and 375 px on 11 Oct 2026: 2,033 formulas in the four lessons, none wider than the column, no TeX errors.

open_obligations: Not yet in the course: flows and the completion of a pretree, quotients, the pretree of cut points of a continuum and its dendritic quotient (Bowditch, Sections 3-5).
